content:
Tai chi is low-impact and can be adapted for painful joints.

This guide explains how to get started safely. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why tai chi may help

  • Improves balance and coordination.
  • Gentle strength work.
  • Can build confidence.

Adapting for arthritis and frailty

  • Use a chair for support or do seated tai chi.
  • Keep knees softly bent, not deep.
  • Rest when needed.
  • Move within comfort.

Finding a class

Ask your GP, falls service or local council about classes. Some are designed for falls prevention.

Combining with other exercise

Strength and balance exercise is recommended for falls prevention.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can I do it seated?

Yes, seated versions exist.

How often?

Regular practice helps most.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: A guide to tai chi
  • NHS: Balance exercises
  • NHS: Falls
